action_types.name: Standard Action
action_types.summary: The main 'do something' action of your turn; one per round.
action_types.details: Attacking, using a skill, advantage, or power, and similar active efforts take a standard action. Each turn you normally get one standard action plus one move action. You may trade the standard action for a second move action (or for a free action).

action_types.name: Move Action
action_types.summary: Moving your speed or doing something of similar duration.
action_types.details: A move action covers moving up to your speed rank, drawing or putting away an item, standing up, picking something up, and comparable tasks. It can come before or after your standard action, but you cannot normally split it around the standard action. Trading your standard action lets you take two move actions in a turn.

action_types.name: Free Action
action_types.summary: Something so quick it takes no meaningful time; take as many as the GM allows on your turn.
action_types.details: Examples include speaking a sentence or two, dropping an object, dropping prone, and ceasing to concentrate on (or ending) a power. Free actions are a conscious choice made on your own turn and can be taken alongside other actions.

action_types.name: Reaction
action_types.summary: An instant response to a trigger, usable even outside your turn.
action_types.details: Reactions take no real time and do not count against your action allotment; you can react as often as circumstances call for, but only when they call for it. Unlike a free action, a reaction responds to something happening and need not occur on your turn. Spending a hero point is normally a reaction.

action_types.name: No Action
action_types.summary: Things like resistance checks that involve no effort from the character.
action_types.details: Some rolls, notably resistance checks, are not actions at all and do not use up any part of your turn. Delaying your turn is also treated as no action.

actions.name: Aid
actions.summary: Help an ally fighting an opponent you could also attack.
actions.details: Make an attack check against DC 10 (you do not actually hit the foe). On a success your ally gains your choice of a +2 circumstance bonus to attack checks against that opponent or a +2 circumstance bonus to defense against it, lasting until the end of the ally's next turn. Four or more degrees of success raise the bonus to +5.

actions.name: Aim
actions.summary: Spend time lining up a shot for a bonus on your next attack.
actions.details: A close attack, or a ranged attack at close range, gains a +5 circumstance bonus; a ranged attack from farther away gains +2. You are vulnerable while aiming and must spend a free action to hold your aim. Your very next action must be the attack, or the bonus is lost.

actions.name: Attack
actions.summary: Make an attack check against an opponent within range.
actions.details: Roll d20 + attack bonus against the target's defense class (10 + Parry for close, 10 + Dodge for ranged). Area and perception-range effects need no attack check; they simply affect the target or area. A natural 20 always hits (and may be a critical hit); a natural 1 always misses.

actions.name: Charge
actions.summary: Rush in a fairly straight line and make a close attack at the end.
actions.details: Move up to your speed rank toward the target using any movement mode you have, then make a close attack at a -2 circumstance penalty. Pairing it with your move action lets you cover up to twice your speed (speed rank for the move, then speed rank again with the charge). Charging is the basis of the Slam Attack maneuver.

actions.name: Command
actions.summary: Give orders to a minion or thrall under your control.
actions.details: Each command to a controlled character, or to a group receiving the same order, takes one move action. Giving different orders to different characters or groups needs a separate move action for each, so you can issue at most two commands in a round.

actions.name: Crawl
actions.summary: Move while prone.
actions.details: A prone character can only crawl, at ground speed -1 rank (half normal speed). Characters with the Slither Movement effect crawl at their full ground speed.

actions.name: Defend
actions.summary: Give up attacking to actively avoid incoming attacks.
actions.details: Until the start of your next turn, every attack against you is resolved as an opposed check: you roll your relevant active defense, adding 10 to any die roll of 10 or less (so the minimum roll is 11, like a hero point re-roll). An attacker must equal or beat your result to hit.

actions.name: Delay
actions.summary: Postpone your whole turn to a later point in the initiative order.
actions.details: You must delay the entire turn and cannot do so after acting or while unable to act. After any other character acts you may step in; your initiative moves to that point. If your next initiative count comes around first, the delayed turn is lost. Beneficial 'until end of turn' effects end when you delay, but harmful ones last until you act, and resistance checks wait until after your turn.

actions.name: Demoralize
actions.summary: Use Intimidation to shake a foe's confidence in combat.
actions.details: Make an Intimidation check opposed by the better of the target's Insight or Will. Success leaves the target impaired (-2 on checks) until the end of your next round; four or more degrees of success leave it disabled (-5) for the same time. Some advantages let Deception substitute for Intimidation here.

actions.name: Disarm
actions.summary: Knock a weapon or device out of an opponent's grip.
actions.details: Attack the defender at -2 (or -5 if using a ranged attack). If you hit, make an opposed check of your attack's damage rank against the defender's Strength; winning makes them drop the item, and an unarmed disarmer can grab it as a free action. If you used a melee weapon and lose, the defender may immediately try to disarm you as a reaction (no further counter by you if that fails).

actions.name: Drop an Item
actions.summary: Let go of something you are holding.
actions.details: Simply releasing an item costs only a free action. Dropping or throwing an object deliberately to hit something is instead a standard attack action.

actions.name: Drop Prone
actions.summary: Fall flat to the ground.
actions.details: Going prone is a free action, but getting back up takes a move action (see Stand). While prone you suffer -5 on close attacks, close attackers get +5 against you, ranged attackers take -5, and you are hindered.

actions.name: Escape
actions.summary: Break free of an opponent's grab.
actions.details: Roll Athletics or Sleight of Hand against the routine result (rank + 10) of the grabber's Strength or grabbing effect rank. Success ends the grab, and you may move away at up to your ground speed -1 rank. Failure means you remain held.

actions.name: Feint
actions.summary: Use Deception to mislead a foe and open them up to your next attack.
actions.details: Make a Deception check (a deception is normally opposed by the target's Deception or Insight). On a success the target is vulnerable against your next attack until the end of your next round. Advantages such as Agile Feint or Startle let other traits (Acrobatics, Speed, Intimidation) stand in for Deception.

actions.name: Grab
actions.summary: Seize and hold a target.
actions.details: Make an attack check; if it hits, the target resists your Strength (or grab effect rank) using the better of its Strength or Dodge. One degree of success leaves it restrained (immobile and vulnerable); two or more leave it bound (defenseless, immobile, impaired). Later grab actions can add cumulative degrees, but a loss lets the target escape. While holding someone you are hindered and vulnerable; maintaining the hold is a free action, letting you spend a standard action to inflict Strength damage on the held target.

actions.name: Move
actions.summary: Travel up to your speed rank.
actions.details: Move your speed rank in any movement mode you possess; ordinary ground speed is rank 0 (about 30 feet). Taking two move actions lets you move your speed rank twice. You cannot normally split a move around your standard action.

actions.name: Ready
actions.summary: Prepare an action to fire off when a stated trigger occurs.
actions.details: Name a single standard, move, or free action and the circumstance that will trigger it; before your next turn you may take it as a reaction when that happens, and your initiative shifts to that point. Since ready is a standard action you may still move. If your next turn arrives first, the readied action is lost (you may ready again). Readying is how you counter an opponent's power.

actions.name: Recover
actions.summary: Catch your breath to shed damage or fatigue, once per conflict.
actions.details: Spend your whole turn recovering: remove your worst level of damage or fatigue, or instead make an extra resistance check against an ongoing effect (on top of the usual end-of-turn check). You also gain +2 circumstance bonus to active defenses until the start of your next turn. Usable only once per conflict.

actions.name: Smash
actions.summary: Attack an object held or worn by an opponent.
actions.details: Make an attack check against the defense of the character carrying the object, with an extra -5 circumstance penalty if the object is held. A hit damages the object instead of the character (see Damaging Objects).

actions.name: Stand
actions.summary: Get up from prone.
actions.details: Standing normally takes a move action. You may instead try a DC 20 Acrobatics check to stand as a free action; if it fails, you can still stand with a move action. The Instant Up advantage lets you stand as a free action with no check.

actions.name: Trick
actions.summary: Use Deception to lure a foe into a dangerous blunder.
actions.details: Make a Deception check opposed by the target's Deception or Insight. Success means the opponent ignores a hazard you set up (a ledge, a live junction box) and may suffer it if their attack on you misses. More than one degree of failure leaves you vulnerable to that target until the start of your next round.

actions.name: Trip
actions.summary: Knock or throw an opponent to the ground.
actions.details: Make a close attack against Parry at -2. If it hits, make an opposed check using the better of Acrobatics or Athletics on each side. If you win, the defender falls prone in an adjacent space of your choice; if you lose, the defender immediately gets an opposed check to trip you in return, and the attempt ends if that fails.

maneuvers.name: Accurate Attack
maneuvers.details: Take up to -2 on the attack's effect modifier and add the same amount (max +2) to your attack bonus. The effect modifier cannot drop below +0 and the attack bonus cannot more than double. Declare before rolling; the change lasts until the start of your next turn.

maneuvers.name: All-out Attack
maneuvers.details: Take up to -2 on your active defenses (Dodge and Parry) and add the same amount (max +2) to your attack bonus. Defenses cannot drop below +0 and the attack bonus cannot more than double. Declare before rolling; it lasts until the start of your next turn.

maneuvers.name: Defensive Attack
maneuvers.details: Take up to -2 on your attack bonus and add the same amount (max +2) to both Dodge and Parry. The attack bonus cannot go below +0 and defenses cannot more than double. Lasts until the start of your next turn. Not usable with effects that need no attack check or allow no resistance check.

maneuvers.name: Finishing Attack
maneuvers.summary: Attack a defenseless target as a routine check, or roll for an automatic critical.
maneuvers.details: Against a defenseless target in close range you may treat the attack as a routine check, which usually means an automatic hit. If you roll normally against DC 10 instead, any hit counts as a critical hit. If you hit with a damaging attack intending to kill and the target's resistance check has three or more degrees of failure, the target dies immediately.

maneuvers.name: Power Attack
maneuvers.details: Take up to -2 on your attack bonus and add the same amount (max +2) to the attack's effect bonus. The attack bonus cannot go below +0 and the effect bonus cannot more than double. Decide before rolling; it lasts until the start of your next turn. Not usable with effects that need no attack check or allow no resistance check.

maneuvers.name: Slam Attack
maneuvers.summary: Charge straight into a target, using momentum as damage.
maneuvers.details: When charging, your damage rank is the higher of your movement speed rank or your normal damage +1. Moving your full speed first adds another +1. Base slam damage (before circumstance modifiers) is capped by power level. You resist half the attack's damage rank (rounded down) with Toughness yourself. Immunity to your own slam damage is Immunity rank 2; Immunity to all slam damage is rank 5.

maneuvers.name: Surprise Attack
maneuvers.summary: An attack that catches the target off guard makes it vulnerable.
maneuvers.details: A surprised target is vulnerable (active defenses halved). Surprise attacks happen in the surprise round, through stealth or concealment, or when the GM rules an unusual tactic (such as an Indirect attack) caught the target unprepared.

maneuvers.name: Team Attack
maneuvers.summary: Several attackers combine similar attacks to overwhelm a target's resistance.
maneuvers.details: Attacks must share the same effect and resistance and be within 5 ranks of one another, and all attackers delay to the slowest attacker's initiative. Each rolls to hit; use the largest effect rank that hit as the main attack. The other hits add up degrees of success: one degree gives +2 to the main attack's rank, three or more give +5. Misses simply add nothing (unlike team checks, they impose no penalty). Effects with no attack check count as one degree of success when not the main attack.

checks.name: Core Mechanic
checks.summary: Roll d20, add modifiers, and compare to a difficulty class.
checks.details: Whenever the outcome is uncertain, roll d20 + the relevant trait rank + any modifiers. Meeting or beating the DC is a success; falling short is a failure.

checks.name: Degrees of Success
checks.summary: Every full 5 points above or below the DC adds another degree.
checks.details: Simply succeeding or failing is one degree; each additional full 5 points over or under the DC adds a degree (fractions dropped). So DC+5 = two successes, DC+10 = three, DC+15 = four; DC-5 = two failures, DC-10 = three, DC-15 = four (e.g. against DC 20: 35 / 30 / 25 / 20 succeed, 15 / 10 / 5 / 0 fail). There is no cap, though beyond two degrees of failure extra degrees seldom matter.

checks.name: Critical Success
checks.summary: A natural 20 raises the result by one degree of success.
checks.details: Work out the degree normally, then improve it by one; this can turn a failure into a success. On an attack check a natural 20 is handled as a critical hit (see Critical Hits).

checks.name: Routine Checks
checks.summary: When not under pressure, treat the die as a 10 instead of rolling.
checks.details: The GM decides when a situation is routine. A routine check result is modifier + 10, so a +0 modifier succeeds at DC 10 and a +10 modifier reaches 20. If the routine result is too low, you may still choose to roll, since the task is not routine for you.

checks.name: Opposed Checks
checks.summary: Both sides roll; the higher result wins.
checks.details: Each character rolls the relevant check and the higher total wins. On a tie, the higher bonus wins; if bonuses also match, roll d20 with 1-10 going to one side and 11-20 to the other (assigned before rolling).

checks.name: Routine Opposition
checks.summary: If one side isn't actively resisting, its check is treated as a routine 10 + modifier.
checks.details: An unaware or unfocused opponent provides a DC of their modifier + 10. This is why attack checks target 10 + defense: active defenses in combat are routine opposition unless the defender takes the Defend action.

checks.name: Comparison Checks
checks.summary: Straight contests of rank with no luck involved: higher rank wins.
checks.details: When it is purely a question of who is stronger or faster, compare ranks instead of rolling. Extra effort and maneuvers can still change the outcome. Identical ranks: roll d20, 1-10 first character, 11-20 the second.

checks.name: Circumstance Modifiers
checks.summary: +/-2 for a favorable/unfavorable situation, +/-5 for a major one.
checks.details: The GM applies circumstance bonuses or penalties to the check result. Lacking necessary tools is a -5 penalty (if the task is possible at all); improvised tools reduce that to -2.

checks.name: Team Checks
checks.summary: Helpers roll against DC 10 to boost a leader's check.
checks.details: The leader (usually the best at the task) rolls normally while each helper makes the same check against DC 10. Total all helpers' degrees: one total degree of success gives the leader +2, three or more give +5; one degree of failure has no effect, two or more impose -2. The leader's modifier is capped at +5 / -2 regardless of the number of helpers, and the GM limits how many can help.

checks.name: Attack Checks
checks.summary: d20 + attack bonus against the target's defense class.
checks.details: Close attacks target Parry and ranged attacks target Dodge (defense class = 10 + defense rank). Meeting or beating it is a hit. A natural 20 always hits and threatens a critical; a natural 1 always misses.

checks.name: Resistance Checks
checks.summary: d20 + the appropriate defense against the effect's DC.
checks.details: Resistance uses Dodge, Fortitude, Toughness, or Will against a DC that is usually the effect rank + 10 (Damage uses rank + 15). Results are often graded, with worse conditions at more degrees of failure. Ongoing effects are re-checked at the end of each of the target's turns; success ends them.

checks.name: Extra Effort
checks.summary: Push beyond your limits for one benefit per turn, at the cost of fatigue.
checks.details: Declare it as a free action, once per turn, for one of: an extra standard action; a +2 circumstance bonus on one check (or upgrade +2 to +5, or reduce a -2 penalty to 0 / a -5 to -2); +1 rank to one power effect until your next turn; a power stunt (temporary Alternate Effect for the scene); an immediate extra resistance check against an ongoing effect; a retry of an effect that requires it; +1 speed rank; or +1 Strength rank until your next turn. Permanent effects cannot be boosted or stunted. At the start of your next turn you become fatigued (fatigued becomes exhausted, exhausted becomes incapacitated) unless you spend a hero point then to cancel it. Extra effort is not limited by power level.

checks.name: Hero Points
checks.summary: Spendable narrative resource; each player starts every session with 1.
checks.details: Spending one is a reaction and you may spend as many as you have. Uses: Edit Scene (add a helpful detail, GM approval); Heroic Feat (one rank of a non-Fortune advantage you lack, until the end of your next turn); Improve Roll (re-roll and keep the better, with 1-10 on the re-roll counting as 11-20; spend before the GM announces the result); Inspiration (a hint or clue from the GM); Instant Counter (counter an effect as a reaction); Recover (instantly remove dazed, fatigued, or stunned, or turn exhausted into fatigued). Unspent points do not carry over; more are earned through complications, heroism, and roleplaying.

checks.name: Initiative
checks.summary: d20 + initiative modifier (base Agility) sets turn order at the start of a conflict.
checks.details: Characters act from highest result to lowest. Ties go to higher Agility, then higher Awareness, then a die roll. The GM may roll once for a whole group of minions. Late arrivals roll when they join and slot into the existing order.

checks.name: Surprise Round
checks.summary: Unaware characters lose the first round.
checks.details: If anyone is surprised, the conflict opens with a surprise round. Surprised characters cannot act and are stunned and vulnerable until the next round; everyone else may take only a standard action (or a move action instead) plus free actions.

combat.name: Taking Your Turn
combat.summary: What happens at the start and end of each turn.
combat.details: At the start of your turn, end any effects lasting 'until the start of your next turn'. Then declare and resolve your actions in any order, without splitting them. At the end, end effects lasting 'until the end of your turn' and make resistance checks to recover from ongoing effects.

combat.name: Critical Hits
combat.summary: A natural 20 that would also have hit by total is a critical hit.
combat.details: A natural 20 always hits and is a threat; if the total also meets the target's defense it is a critical hit, otherwise a normal hit (Improved Critical widens the threat range, but only a natural 20 auto-hits). Choose one benefit: Increased Effect (+5 to the resistance DC; a minion automatically suffers the worst degree), Added Effect (a second rank-0 effect such as an Affliction, resisted at DC 10, or 15 for Damage), or Alternate Effect (like a free power stunt with no fatigue).

combat.name: Concealment
combat.summary: Penalties for attacking what you cannot clearly perceive.
combat.details: Partial concealment (dim light, fog, foliage, smoke) imposes -2 on attack checks; total concealment (darkness, heavy smoke) imposes -5, assuming you even know where to aim.

combat.name: Cover
combat.summary: Penalties for attacking a target behind physical obstructions.
combat.details: Partial cover (roughly half the target obscured) imposes -2 on attack checks; total cover (three-quarters or more) imposes -5. A target completely behind cover cannot be attacked, though the cover itself can. Cover also adds the same value as a bonus to Dodge checks against area effects originating from the far side.

combat.name: Defense Class
combat.summary: Your active defense + 10 is the DC to hit you.
combat.details: Close attacks target 10 + Parry, ranged attacks 10 + Dodge. Vulnerable halves active defenses (round up); defenseless reduces them to 0, so the DC is just 10 and attackers may roll as routine checks.

combat.name: Perception and Area Effects
combat.summary: Automatic effects that skip the attack check.
combat.details: Perception-range and area effects hit automatically, so they cannot score critical hits or misses and are unaffected by maneuvers or other modifiers to attack checks. Area effects usually allow a Dodge check for reduced effect.

combat.name: Minions
combat.summary: Special rules that make minor foes easy to defeat.
combat.details: Minions cannot score critical hits on non-minions. Non-minions may attack minions as routine checks. A minion that fails a resistance check suffers the effect's worst degree (e.g. any failed Damage check incapacitates). Some traits, such as Takedown, work especially well against them.

combat.name: Ongoing Effects
combat.summary: Some effects are resisted repeatedly until shaken off.
combat.details: The target makes a resistance check at the end of each of its turns; success ends the effect and its conditions, failure means they persist as the effect describes.

combat.name: Damaging Objects
combat.summary: Inanimate objects are defenseless and break on bad resistance checks.
combat.details: Objects ignore dazed and staggered (constructs do not). Being defenseless, they can be attacked with a finishing attack: routine check, or roll normally for an automatic critical (+5 effect). When trying to break something, two degrees of failure on its Toughness check is a break and three or more destroys it.

combat.name: Death
combat.summary: Main characters only die after being incapacitated and then deliberately harmed further.
combat.details: An incapacitated character who fails another Damage resistance check becomes dying; a dying character who fails one is dead. Dying characters roll Fortitude DC 15 each round (two degrees of success stabilizes, three total degrees of failure is death); a DC 15 Treatment check or Healing can stabilize them. Minions can be killed by any successful attack made with that intent.

difficulty.label: Easy
difficulty.example: Climb a rope with knots in it (Athletics)

difficulty.label: Formidable
difficulty.example: Scale a slick, wet rock face (Athletics)

difficulty.label: Super-heroic
difficulty.example: Talk your way past guards with no ID or clearance (Deception)

difficulty.label: Nigh-impossible
difficulty.example: Track a trained commando through jungle on a dark night after days of rain (Perception)

results.result: -1 circumstance penalty to further Toughness checks against damage.
Dazed until the end of the target's next turn, plus a -1 penalty to further damage resistance checks.
Staggered (dazed and hindered) until recovered, plus a -1 penalty to further damage resistance checks. Being staggered a second time (another three-degree failure) applies the fourth degree instead.

damage.notes: The -1 penalties stack (three failed checks of one to three degrees each = -3 total). An incapacitated target who fails another Damage check becomes dying; a dying target who fails one dies. Minions that fail any Damage resistance check are incapacitated. Objects being deliberately broken suffer a break at two degrees of failure and are destroyed at three or more. Strength provides built-in close Damage equal to its rank.

afflictions: The target resists with Fortitude or Will (set when the power is bought; some use Dodge for the initial check) against DC Affliction rank + 10. Success: no effect. One degree of failure imposes the first-degree condition (choose one of dazed, entranced, fatigued, hindered, impaired, or vulnerable); two degrees impose the second (compelled, defenseless, disabled, exhausted, immobile, prone, or stunned); three degrees impose the third (asleep, controlled, incapacitated, paralyzed, transformed, or unaware). The conditions for each degree are fixed when the power is created. First- and second-degree conditions can be shaken off with a resistance check at the end of each of the target's turns; third-degree conditions need a minute of recovery or outside help such as Treatment or Healing (DC 10 + rank). Repeated hits are not cumulative unless the power has the Cumulative extra; a later, higher-degree result replaces the earlier one. (DCA 87)

measurement_notes.name: Using the Measurements Table
measurement_notes.summary: Each rank roughly doubles the previous one; ranks convert to real-world mass, time, distance, and volume.
measurement_notes.details: Each +1 rank beyond 30 doubles the value; each rank below -5 halves it. A rank covers a span, so round a value up to the next listed entry (12 hours is time rank 13). Never add ranks directly: convert to measures, add, and convert back. Handy formulas: Distance rank = Time rank + Speed rank; Time rank = Distance rank - Speed rank; Throwing distance rank = Strength rank - mass rank of the object. Lifting capacity is the mass for your Strength rank (Strength 3 = 400 lbs.).

hazards.name: Falling
hazards.summary: Damage based on how far you fall.
hazards.details: A fall deals Damage rank 4 + twice the distance rank fallen, up to a maximum of rank 16. Acrobatics can let you fall farther safely, and landing on something dangerous may add damage. Catching a falling person or object takes a DC 5 Dexterity check; subtract your Strength (or, with GM approval, a power such as Flight or Move Object) from the fall damage, and both of you resist whatever remains.

hazards.name: Heat & Cold
hazards.summary: Exposure forces repeated Fortitude checks against fatigue.
hazards.details: Make a Fortitude check (DC 10, +1 per previous check) at the end of each exposure period: every hour for uncomfortable conditions, every 10 minutes for intense (desert, arctic), every minute for extreme (volcano edge, arctic storm). Failures progress fatigued, exhausted, incapacitated, then dying. Truly intense sources (blast furnace, liquid nitrogen) deal direct damage like an attack. Appropriate Immunity removes the need to check.

hazards.name: Light & Darkness
hazards.details: Dim or dark areas give targets concealment: partial concealment is -2 to attack checks, total concealment (complete darkness) is -5. Senses that counter concealment from darkness ignore these penalties.

hazards.name: Starvation & Thirst
hazards.summary: Going without water or food leads to escalating fatigue.
hazards.details: Without water, after one day make a Fortitude check (DC 10, +1 per previous check) every hour or gain a level of fatigue. Without food, after three days make the same check every day. You cannot recover until you get water or food. Immunity to Starvation and Thirst removes the need.

hazards.name: Suffocation
hazards.summary: Holding your breath, then risking incapacitation and death.
hazards.details: You can hold your breath for 10 rounds (one minute) plus rounds equal to twice your Stamina. After that, make a Fortitude check each round at DC 10, +1 per previous success. On a failure you are incapacitated, and the following round you are dying; you cannot stabilize until you can breathe. Immunity to Suffocation lets you go without air indefinitely.

hazards.name: Drowning
hazards.summary: Being underwater uses the Suffocation rules.
hazards.details: Swimming takes a DC 10 Athletics check (move action) to move at ground speed -2 ranks; a failure means no progress and more than one degree of failure means you go under. Underwater you must hold your breath and follow the Suffocation rules. Immunity (Drowning) or Immunity to Suffocation negates it.

hazards.name: Vacuum
hazards.summary: The bends, lung damage, suffocation, and radiation in open space.
hazards.details: Starting on the third round of exposure, make a DC 20 Fortitude check each round or suffer the bends: stunned until back at normal pressure, or incapacitated with two or more degrees of failure. Holding your breath in vacuum takes a Fortitude check each round starting at DC 15 and rising by 1 per round; each success still costs a rank of Stamina, and a failure (or exhaling) starts suffocation: incapacitated the next round, dying the round after, unable to stabilize until back in atmosphere. Unprotected characters are also exposed to radiation. Surviving deep space requires Immunity to Suffocation, Vacuum, and Radiation at minimum.

Diseases are typically Affliction or Weaken effects, sometimes Linked. Lethal diseases tend to Weaken Stamina, and dropping below Stamina -5 means death. Immunity to Disease negates them, and Treatment can grant a bonus on resistance checks.

hazards.summary: Toxins usually work as Affliction, Damage, or Weaken, resisted by Fortitude.
hazards.details: Poisons may enter through a wound or the air and are generally Affliction, Damage, or Weaken effects, sometimes several Linked together. Fortitude is the usual resistance (DC 10 + rank; 15 + rank for Damage). Immunity to Poison negates them entirely, and Treatment can give a bonus on resistance checks.

hazards.name: Radiation
hazards.summary: Handled like a disease: initial and daily Fortitude checks.
hazards.details: In comics radiation is as likely to cause mutations or awaken powers as sickness, making it a good complication. Otherwise treat it like disease: a Fortitude check against DC 10 + radiation rank on exposure and again each day. Radiation sickness is usually Weaken Stamina, possibly with Fortitude-resisted Damage or temporary loss of power ranks at the GM's discretion.

hazards.name: Fire
hazards.summary: Sample Damage ranks for common fire sources.
hazards.details: The book gives fire only as a table of sample ranks; treat a fire source as a Damage effect of the listed rank (Toughness vs. DC 15 + rank). Intense heat sources deal direct damage like an attack (see Heat & Cold).

recovery: Damage: living characters remove one damage condition per minute of rest, worst first, so incapacitated, then staggered, then dazed, then each -1 Toughness penalty, one per minute (Healing and Regeneration speed this up). Objects do not recover on their own and must be repaired (Technology). In combat, the Recover action (once per conflict, takes your turn) removes your worst level of damage or fatigue or grants an extra resistance check, plus +2 to active defenses until your next turn. A hero point instantly removes dazed, fatigued, or stunned, or turns exhausted into fatigued. Fatigued clears after an hour of rest; exhausted after an hour of rest in comfortable surroundings. Ongoing effects (including Affliction first/second degrees) are resisted at the end of each turn; third-degree Affliction conditions take a minute or outside aid. A dying character stabilizes with two degrees of success on the DC 15 Fortitude check or a DC 15 Treatment check. (DCA 18-21, 87, 177, 179)
range: Every attack is close, ranged, or perception range. Close attacks only reach targets you can physically touch or hit with a melee weapon. Ranged attacks have three bands: short range up to rank x 25 feet (no penalty), medium up to rank x 50 feet (-2 to the attack check), and long up to rank x 100 feet (-5); beyond long range you cannot attack. Perception-range attacks automatically affect any target you can accurately perceive, with no attack check. Otherwise the game only tracks whether characters are adjacent (close range) and whether they can perceive one another. (DCA 172-173)

stance_rules.summary: Everyone starts in the Neutral stance. Changing stance is a Close Combat or Ranged Combat: Fighting Style check against the stance's DC; one stance at a time.
rules: Everyone is assumed to be in a Neutral stance to begin with, even characters who know no fighting style.

Changing stances requires a Close Combat or Ranged Combat (as appropriate): Fighting Style check as a move action, or a free action when switching from the Neutral stance. The check's DC is that of the stance being attempted.
Assuming a Neutral stance needs no check and is automatic.
Failing the check to assume a new stance automatically puts the character into the Neutral stance.
A stance's benefits and detriments apply until the stance is disrupted or switched. No check is made each round to maintain it, only to switch or to re-assume a disrupted stance.

The asleep, defenseless, immobile, incapacitated, paralyzed, prone, stunned and vulnerable conditions disrupt the stance and return the character to Neutral. Ending an encounter usually returns a character to Neutral.
A character may assume only one stance at a time. Stance benefits remain limited by the game's PL maximums.

A stance of one style can be used for another style only if a rank of the (Style) Stances advantage is also taken for that style, the styles share the same type of stance, and the character announces the switch of style as a free action. A new Fighting Style check is then required to maintain the stance under the new style.
A Gamemaster may let a non-martial artist buy a single stance as an advantage; they then use a Fighting check instead, and the stance's DC rises by 10.
stance_rules.identify: Close Combat or Ranged Combat: Fighting Style or Expertise: Specific Fighting Style (stance DC +5, Neutral automatic); free action; +2 DC per extra stance in a round; line of sight needed.
stance_rules.disrupt: Declare a disruptive attack (-5 attack, -2 Damage); if it lands, opposed Fighting Style checks; the loser's stance becomes Neutral.

optional_rules.name: Hit Location
optional_rules.summary: Inevitably, a player is going to ask the Gamemaster to strike a particular part of an opponent with an attack, be it with a fist, bullet, or energy blast. The core rules contain no express method for determining the chance of hitting a particular target, let alone what effect may result if successful.
optional_rules.text: Inevitably, a player is going to ask the Gamemaster to strike a particular part of an opponent with an attack, be it with a fist, bullet, or energy blast. The core rules contain no express method for determining the chance of hitting a particular target, let alone what effect may result if successful. As such, Gamemasters tend to handle the situation in one of two ways: 1) They improvise the whole thing by imposing a penalty to hit that seems about right and then makes up any additional results if successful. 2) They maintain the entire process is thematic and, although altering the description of what happens to suit the player's choice. As such, they don't allow any additional results. Although either of these two methods will solve the issue just fine (not to mention any of the other techniques a Gamemaster may employ), sometimes a more definitive option may be what's called for. Hit Location 1d20 Location Attack Effect Rank * 1-2 Feet -4 x0.5 3-5 Leg -2 x 1 6-7 Vitals -8 x 1.5 8-11 Abdomen -4 x 1 12-15 Chest -2 x 1 16-17 Head -4 x 2 18-19 Arm -4 x 1 20 Hand -8 x 0.5 * Round down to a minimum of 1 rank Generally, the Gamemaster should only rule that a particular location on the target has been struck if that was the attacker's intentions. If no such intention is expressed, hit location should be nothing more than a matter of storytelling so combat progresses normally. In some circumstances, however, the Gamemaster may wish to roll randomly to determine which specific location was struck to add a bit of drama and suspense. Should the attacker decide to attack a specific part of the target, however, consult the Hit Location table to find out how difficult the attempt will be and how the attack's Damage rank is modified (rounded down). This modifier does not affect the attack's range or any other aspects related to its rank. If the effect is not damaging but is of the sort the Gamemaster feels may still benefit from hit location, multiply the effect's rank by the Damage modifier. Again, this modified rank only applies to effect, resistance check DC, and the like. The modifier still does not alter the effect's range, duration, etc. If the attack successfully strikes the desired location, consult the following location descriptions to see what sort of additional effects come in to play. A miss, on the other hand, can be handled in one of three ways: Miss Option 1) The attack misses the target altogether. Miss Option 2) The attack doesn't strike the desired location, but if it would normally have been sufficient to hit the target, in general, it will still do so in this instance. Proceed with determining the outcome as per standard combat. Miss Option 3) The attack doesn't strike the desired location, but if it would normally have been sufficient to hit the target, in general, proceed to the Unintended Hit Location table and roll 1d20 to see where the attack hit instead. A result of "standard" means no specific location was struck and the outcome should be determined as per standard combat. The miss option you decide to utilize should become the standard for the game--don't go switching back and forth between them on separate occasions. To do so risks the players not knowing what to expect of the rules, and thus they'll have difficulty playing within them. Make a choice and stick with it, suiting your personal tastes and desired level of realism. Considering all the possible mutations and alien species that are typical of the super-heroic genre, Gamemaster may be called upon to adjust attack penalties and/or effects of hitting a particular location belonging to an abnormal physiology and anatomy. For example, the Gamemaster may decide a mutant with two heads won't suffer any of the usual hit location effects from damage to just one head because the other remains unharmed. Similarly, possessing powers that make the target's nerves especially sensitive may result in additional effects if the related sensory organ is damaged. Alternate Effects by Location The rules regarding striking specific locations (and the effects of such) assume the target to be human, or near enough as not to matter. As such, the effects of hitting specific locations that may be targeted, along with all mechanics involving the probability of striking these areas, may not suit non-human targets, although most animals shouldn't pose a problem. When facing creatures with radically different anatomical and physiological characteristics, the Gamemaster will be called upon to use their best judgment to adjust these rules on the fly. A creature with more than two arms, for example, would mean the chance of hitting an arm while aiming for and missing the chest would likely increase. Accounting for proportioned differences in size is already accommodated in the standard combat rules, but if a part of a target's anatomy is especially disproportionate relative to the rest of the body (an exceptionally overor under-sized head, for instance), the Gamemaster should similarly adjust the location's attack modifier accordingly. Some targets will possess choice locations just begging to be singled out for targeting, but are entirely alien to the human body and thus not represented in these rules. Attacking a dragon's tail, for example, is a situation beyond the scope of the basic hit location rules. In such instances, the Gamemaster should look to the existing rules as guidelines for determining both the attack modifier and effects of success. Begin to do so by comparing the location's size to those already provided when determining the attack modifier, and then use a balance of common sense and imagination when it comes to the effect. optional_rules.name: Vehicle Hit Location
optional_rules.summary: Hit Location Just as with living creatures, vehicles may be targeted or inadvertently struck in specific locations. Although each vehicle will vary, the constraints of space limit this work to a few generalized hit location tables and effects.
optional_rules.text: Hit Location Just as with living creatures, vehicles may be targeted or inadvertently struck in specific locations. Although each vehicle will vary, the constraints of space limit this work to a few generalized hit location tables and effects. Beyond these simplified game mechanics, the Gamemaster should feel free to make their own or customize those presented here. If the attack roll is not sufficient to strike the desired specific location but would have otherwise been high enough to succeed with a normal attack had the hit location penalty not been applied, roll on the following table to see what happens to the failed attack. Vehicle Hit Location Damage Results Unless otherwise stated, the following damage results are in addition to the standard results of the damage condition. These results remain in effect until proper repairs are made. Effects that don't cause damage but are ruled to be modified by hit location pay no mind to the following effects. Instead, they restrict themselves to the rank multiplier presented in the hit location table (pg 109), applying the multiplier to their ranks for the purpose of the effect only (do not adjust range, duration, etc.) If a vehicle hit location damage result indicates a reduction in Toughness, and the Toughness is reduced to 0, the vehicle is still holding together. However, it makes it much more difficult for the vehicle to keep functioning following additional successful attacks against it. All effects are cumulative with damage effects previously acquired, opting for the most serious condition where they may conflict. Adornment A vehicle's adornments includes side view mirrors, spoilers, radio antenna, over-sized mufflers, and anything else that is an "option" not vital to the vehicle's function and performance. This can also be used to represent unusual specifics that are important but not otherwise represented on the hit location tables, such as sensor dishes and the like. One Degree of Failure Damaged but still recognizable (and functional, if appropriate). Two or Three Degrees of Failure Damaged to the point where it isn't recognizable (and no longer functions, if appropriate). Four Degrees of Failure Broken clean off or outright destroyed. Body/Fuselage The main (and typically largest) portion of the vehicle, this is the frame to which the other parts are attached or housed within. Engine Unless the vehicle has a wholly or largely exposed engine, such as is the case with a motorcycle, hitting this location only does normal damage instead of multiplying by 1.5. This is because any attack must first penetrate the vehicle's chassis. One Degree of Failure Things aren't working quite right. Reduce the vehicle's effective Strength by 1 rank. Four Degrees of Failure The engine is disabled and the vehicle will come to a halt unless it has more than one engine, in which case reduce speed by the ratio represented by the missing engine. For example, if a vehicle has three engines and one is lost, speed will be reduced by one-third (rounded down). Fuel Tank The internal fuel storage. Treat any external fuel tanks as adornment on the hit location table, but use the following to determine the effects of damage results. One Degree of Failure Small holes in the fuel tank will require refueling in threequarters the usual time. Also, any attacks with appropriate agitating properties (such as flames versus gasoline fuel) has a 10% (1-2 on a d20) chance of igniting any remaining fuel in a Burst Area Damage effect of as many ranks as the vehicle's Strength divided by 4 (round down with a minimum of 1 rank). Such an explosion destroys the fuel tank. Two or Three Degrees of Failure Massive tears and holes in the tank will require refueling in one-quarter the usual time. Also, any attacks with appropriately agitating properties (such as flames versus gasoline fuel) has a 50% (1-10 on a d20) chance of igniting any remaining fuel in a Burst Area Damage effect of as many ranks as the vehicle's Strength divided by 2 (round down with a minimum of 1 rank). Such an explosion destroys the fuel tank. Four Degrees of Failure The fuel tank is damaged to the point of no longer being able to contain any fuel, spilling its contents. The vehicle may operate on what fuel was already in its system for 1d20 more rounds. Also, any attacks with appropriate agitating properties (such as flames versus gasoline fuel) have an 80% (1-16 on a d20) chance of igniting the spilled fuel in a Burst Area Damage effect of as many ranks as the vehicle's Strength. Such an explosion destroys the fuel tank. As with two or three degrees of failure, an attack against the window has a chance of hitting someone inside the vehicle. Rotor Blade A helicopter (or similar vehicle) is kept aloft and directed by one or more rotors. One Degree of Failure One of the blades, the rotor mast, or the like is damaged enough to impede perfect operation. Vehicles checks suffer a -1 penalty. Two or Three Degrees of Failure An entire rotor blade has been destroyed, reducing speed by an amount equal to the fraction the destroyed rotor represented of the total (rounded down). For example, a craft with three rotors that loses one would reduce its Flight ranks by one-third because it has lost one-third of its rotors. Vehicles checks suffer a -4 penalty. At least two rotor blades must remain for the rotor to remain functional. The vehicle will begin to crash if this means a loss of 50% or more of the total rotors. Disabling Critical Hits A common aspect of the martial arts genre is using one's skills against opponents in ways that not only defeat them but are disabling in some fashion. The punch that breaks a nose, the tearing off of an ear, or the joint lock that snaps an arm like dry kindling are all examples of disabling attacks. When an attack roll naturally falls within an attack's critical threat range, a second d20 is rolled if you wish to use this optional rule. Apply to this second d20 all attack modifiers that pertained to the first attack roll. If a 20 or higher result is achieved on this second roll, the critical hit is considered disabling so long as a damaging critical hit also results.

optional_rules.name: Creative Vehicle Combat
optional_rules.summary: Although the focus of this work is what you'd expect from a book entitled Metahuman Martial Arts 3e, it also tackles other aspects of combat, including that which utilizes vehicle (as exemplified by the Drive-Fu fighting style on pg 227). Just how much a Gamemaster wants to focus on these combat alternatives is up for them to decide, but consider moving beyond the traditional role of advantages and skills when doing so.
optional_rules.text: Although the focus of this work is what you'd expect from a book entitled Metahuman Martial Arts 3e, it also tackles other aspects of combat, including that which utilizes vehicle (as exemplified by the Drive-Fu fighting style on pg 227). Just how much a Gamemaster wants to focus on these combat alternatives is up for them to decide, but consider moving beyond the traditional role of advantages and skills when doing so. Consider how the Vehicrobatics advantage (pg 71) extends using the Acrobatics skill to vehicle combat, for example. Similarly, look at the other advantages, skills, and combat rules to consider how they too would apply outside of their standard framework. To get an idea of how existing combat rules may be implemented in new and imaginative ways regarding vehicle combat, consider the act of disarming. Defining a disarm attempt against an opponent wielding a knife is simple: you know he has the knife right there in his hand. The act of disarming him will involve knocking the weapon to the ground or otherwise removing it. Simple, right? But what about disarming a tank? What about a dune buggy-mounted rocket launcher? Would a disarm action apply to either? Rather than just saying no outright because such concepts extend beyond the default presentation in the core rules, the Gamemaster should keep in mind that the idea of the game is to have fun. This sometimes requires adapting to the situation and running with an exciting idea. A Gamemaster may decide that a Wheelman (pg 44) could indeed apply a disarm action against a vehicle, given the right conditions. First off, rules the Gamemaster, the Wheelman will have to use their own vehicle to attempt the disarm. Also, because that vehicle is a sports car, it will work against the dune buggy's rockets (a rather light, fragile arrangement), but not against a tank's main gun (as it is securely housed within a reinforced turret that would tear the car apart). The player behind the Wheelman character explains they will use some creative driving to throw their car into the air, over the dune buggy, using their own vehicle's wheels to knock the rockets off their mounting, thus disarming it. The Gamemaster decides this is an appropriate, creative idea and gives their permission to attempt doing so because the Wheelman is so heavily oriented towards performing extraordinary things with vehicles. And don't think that because the Gamemaster ruled that a disarm action couldn't be used against the tank that they have disallowed all other options. What about applying the Redirect advantage to trick the tank into shooting at the dune buggy as the Wheelman's sports car sails overhead, knocking out its rockets? Similarly, using an Affliction effect intended to knock a target prone (that is to say, trip it) would almost certainly be out of the question against the tank--it's just too heavy and stable. However, what about using the sports car to apply this effect against a motorcycle, such as by plowing the car's front hood into and under the bike's front tire? Sometimes it is okay (even preferred) for the Gamemaster to wholly put what's realistic aside in light of what's fun, especially when what's proposed is creative and bold. Thankfully, the comic book genre encourages this sort of play, as do many of the different styles of martial arts campaigns. So long as the level of realism being aimed for remains consistent so the players know where they stand, the Gamemaster shouldn't feel they are doing anything wrong by relaxing the rules a bit in this fashion, and should instead try encouraging it to see what happens. 6. Art of the Fight The primary purpose of Metahuman Martial Arts 3e is to provide you with new combat options. How could any such product be considered complete without a variety of fighting styles to add some martial flavor to your game? To that end, this chapter includes a broad range of combat maneuvers that will make martial arts a unique and vital aspect of your game. The actual fighting styles created using this system are presented in the chapter to follow. Fighting styles 101 Unlike previous rules and guidelines for representing different martial arts fighting styles for Super-Powered by M&M rules, Metahuman Martial Arts 3e has taken the concept further by adding new, power-like maneuvers, unique combat stances, and more. Doing so allows the fighting styles to become much more than has presented in other publications, offering an entirely new way of looking at fighting styles within the Super-Powered by M&M framework. Unarmed vs. Weapon Fighting Styles Some fighting styles focus on unarmed combat, others with wielding a particular weapon or weapons, while most incorporate both. The distinction between unarmed and weapon fighting styles is largely one of flavor and description, though. Almost all combat and martial arts advantages work the same whether you're using them unarmed, armed or with super-human powers, although a number are specific to a particular attack. new_actions.name: Entangle Weapon
new_actions.summary: If you successfully parry a close combat weapon attack using a close combat weapon of your own possessing a cross guard, dual blades, loose chains, snare wires, or the like, you can make an attempt to entangle the attacker's weapon with your own.
new_actions.details: If you successfully parry a close combat weapon attack using a close combat weapon of your own possessing a cross guard, dual blades, loose chains, snare wires, or the like, you can make an attempt to entangle the attacker's weapon with your own. Do so by proceeding with a disarm action, meaning all modifiers for a disarm apply. Success means the weapon is locked with your own, in your control to maintain the hold or release at will. However, both weapons involved in the maneuver are incapable of being used for anything else so long as the entangle remains. Failure means the target may attempt an entangle weapon maneuver of their own against you as a free action if their weapon is equipped to do so. The initiator of this maneuver can free their weapon at will, but the target may try to escape or reverse the maneuver (or let go of their weapon as a free action, losing it in the process). Doing so requires making an opposed check with both participants choosing to apply either their Strength or disarm modifier (but not both). If the opponent is successful, they may choose to remove their weapon entirely from the entanglement. Alternatively, they may opt to reverse the entanglement, now considering them to be the one in control of the maneuver and the original initiator the subject of it. Whoever is in control of an entangle weapon maneuver may attempt to disarm their opponent as a move action without the usual -2 penalty for a disarm.

new_actions.name: Grab, Body Shield
new_actions.summary: You may twist your grabbed opponent into the way of an incoming attack, gaining cover as though the grabbed opponent's body were an obstacle.
new_actions.details: You may twist your grabbed opponent into the way of an incoming attack, gaining cover as though the grabbed opponent's body were an obstacle. If the attack misses you but does so with only one degree of failure, the grabbed opponent being used as a shield is automatically struck by the attack instead. An opponent of the same size or smaller than you who is being used as a body shield counts as partial cover, and an opponent who is larger than you is considered total cover. You cannot use as a body shield an opponent who is 3 or more ranks smaller than you.

new_actions.name: Grab, Joint Lock
new_actions.summary: Only usable by characters with the Joint Lock advantage, you suffer a -2 penalty to any grab checks against the opponent you are attempting to grab or are already grabbing and holding but are not vulnerable while doing so (you remain hindered, however).
new_actions.details: Only usable by characters with the Joint Lock advantage, you suffer a -2 penalty to any grab checks against the opponent you are attempting to grab or are already grabbing and holding but are not vulnerable while doing so (you remain hindered, however). You do so by leveraging their joints in a way that impedes them. This also imposes a -4 penalty on any checks they make to resist, counter, or escape your grab so long as the joint lock is maintained. New Maneuvers The following includes some optional new maneuvers to employ in your game.

new_actions.name: Impromptu Ranged Attack
new_actions.summary: By making a successful close combat attack check with a -4 penalty against an object of a mass rank on the Measurements table at least 4 ranks below your Strength rank, your attack propels that object, sending it through the air towards the desired target.
new_actions.details: By making a successful close combat attack check with a -4 penalty against an object of a mass rank on the Measurements table at least 4 ranks below your Strength rank, your attack propels that object, sending it through the air towards the desired target. A character with Strength 4 could make an impromptu ranged attack with an object of a mass rank of 0 (50 lbs). or less. This same attack check result is then used to determine if the object strikes its intended target, considering it thrown for the sake of range. The defender is taken by surprise and is considered vulnerable to the attack if they fail an opposed Insight check as a free action against your attack check result. The attack's Damage modifier is equal to the object's mass rank plus your Strength modifier. If this combined Damage modifier exceeds the object's Toughness, the object breaks on impact (with your target or something else if the attack misses).

new_actions.name: Twist It Deep
new_actions.summary: When a piercing melee attack (usually a weapon) successfully strikes an opponent, the attacker may opt to twist the means of attack while it's still in the target before removing it, thus worsening the wound.
new_actions.details: When a piercing melee attack (usually a weapon) successfully strikes an opponent, the attacker may opt to twist the means of attack while it's still in the target before removing it, thus worsening the wound. This twisting action relies upon several conditions being met and counts as a move action. Such a twisting action is considered to strike automatically (meaning no attack roll is needed) because the weapon is already in the target but has a Damage modifier equal to half that of the original piercing attack (round down). However, do not apply the Strength modifier. The attacker suffers a -4 penalty to their defenses until their next action following use of this maneuver. For this maneuver to be possible, the piercing attack cannot be used or otherwise removed between the initial attack and the twisting action. Also, the attacker and opponent must remain within sufficient proximity of each other to allow the twisting action to occur (meaning the attacker can't twist a blade if the opponent moves away or the initial attack causes knockback that takes the target out of reach). New Hot Pursuit & Vehicle Combat Maneuvers The following are maneuvers (stunts) a vehicle's driver or pilot may attempt according to the Hot Pursuit & Vehicle Combat Optional Rules presented in Better Mousetrap 3e. Not all maneuvers may be performed by all types of vehicles, and so each lists the vehicle types that may attempt to perform them.

pursuer.name: Buy Time
pursuer.summary: The pursuer stalls, matches speed, feints, and maneuvers with another vehicle, all with the purpose of setting the latter up for another pursuer maneuver to follow.
pursuer.success: Declare an opponent to use this maneuver against. In the next round, the pursuer increase by +2 any bonuses gained by a maneuver performed that targets the same opponent, be the bonus to initiative, skill checks, dodge, damage, etc.

pursuer.name: Dovetail
pursuer.summary: The pursuer heads towards a target and, at the last moment, swings their vehicle's rear end out towards it by using the front as a pivot. This moves the vehicle in a one hundred and eighty-degree turn on the spot. The vehicle's swinging rear end is intended to strike the target as the turn is made.
pursuer.vehicle_types: Aquatic (surface, submerged), Ground; some aerial vehicles, such as helicopters, may be capable of performing this maneuver
pursuer.success: The pursuer inflicts a slam attack against their target as though the latter had been rammed. However, the Damage modifier applied to both target and vehicle is halved (round down). Increase the required maneuver check's DC by +5 if you wish to knock over a pedestrian or the like with this maneuver rather than ram them. If successful, you inflict an Affliction (Resisted by Dodge; Vulnerable, Prone) Limited Degree effect upon the target. This effect has the same rank as the damage bonus the slam attack would have possessed.

pursuer.name: Pop the Top
pursuer.summary: The pursuer makes their vehicle airborne, aiming it at a target vehicle's crew like a weapon in a clipping attack. This often takes the form of a jumping car using its lower frame and tires to tear through another car's roof, or a plane using a wing or lowered landing gear to clip another plane's cockpit. If the target vehicle is tall enough, the pursuer's vehicle may need to first pull off a jump maneuver.
pursuer.success: The target vehicle suffers half the normal Damage modifier from a slam attack from the pursuer's vehicle, but any of the target vehicle's crew directly in the way suffers the full Damage modifier. The pursuer's vehicle experiences one-third the Damage modifier applied to the target vehicle's crew (rounded down).

pursuer.name: Upper Hand
pursuer.summary: The pursuer attempts to maneuver their vehicle into a position that not only improves their attack's likelihood of striking successfully but also reduces the target's ability to see and/or anticipate the pursuer's vehicle.
pursuer.success: The pursuer gains a +2 bonus to attack the target in the following round. If it is just those two vehicles involved in combat (or if a second roll to break a tie for initiative with the target vehicle), the pursuer also gains

target.name: Barrel Roll
target.summary: The vehicle is put into a rotating spin around a central, long axis, as though spinning while encircling a straight line along the vehicle's path.
target.speed: Reduce pursuit speed by one-quarter (round down), but falling short of no longer moving.
target.success: The target gains a +2 bonus to dodge, but suffer a -4 penalty to any other Vehicles checks during that round.

target.name: Jink
target.summary: The target vehicle moves from side to side (and up and down, if able) at random intervals and angles. It does so to throw off any pursuers or other attackers targeting it.
target.success: Gain a +1 bonus to the target vehicle's dodge for the round per degree of success. Anyone in the vehicle firing weapons suffers a penalty to their own attack rolls equal

either.name: Clip
either.summary: The pursuer or target attempts to clip/nudge another vehicle with the hope of forcing them to lose control.
either.speed: Reduce pursuit speed by one-quarter (round down), but falling short of no longer moving.
either.success: This counts as a ram/slam, but consider the Damage modifier to be one-quarter normal for both vehicles (rounding down). Also, the pursuer or target performing this maneuver forces the other vehicle to make an immediate crash check.

either.name: Half-Wheeler
either.summary: The vehicle is brought up onto one side, raising the other half of itself (and its wheels/skis/whatever) up into the air so the vehicle may slide through space normally too thin for it or to get one side of the vehicle over (or onto) an obstacle. The particulars are up to the Gamemaster to determine, based on the vehicle--cars are fairly easy, whereas a motorcycle would move forward on its front tire, swinging the rear to the side and up, for instance.
either.success: Reduce the vehicle's effective width by half and/or lift the elevated side over an obstacle as tall as the vehicle itself.

either.name: Jump, High
either.summary: The pursuer or target makes their vehicle temporarily airborne via some sort of ramp (or obstacle that will serve as such), with the intention of jumping for height. A maneuver check is required to make the jump, and another to maintain control upon landing it.
either.speed: Reduce pursuit speed by half (round down), but falling short of no longer moving.
either.success: A vehicle may jump a maximum vertical distance in feet (from the top of the ramp) equal to (maneuver check result minus the defense modifier for the vehicle's size) plus the vehicle's current speed rank. A result of 0 or less means the vehicle is not capable of (significantly) jumping at that speed. The jump will also travel a horizontal distance of half (rounded down) as many feet as the vertical jump's height, with a minimum distance of 5 feet traveled horizontally. The vehicle jumps over the wall, also traveling 10 feet horizontally. Failing the maneuver skill check means falling short, twisting sideways or the like, or possibly hitting something you are trying to jump over. either.name: Jump, Long
either.summary: You are able to make the vehicle temporarily airborne via some sort of ramp or obstacle that will serve as such, with the intention of jumping for distance. A maneuver check is required to make the jump, and another to maintain control upon landing it.
either.success: A vehicle may jump a maximum horizontal distance in feet (from the top of the ramp) equal to (maneuver check result minus the defense modifier for the vehicle's size) plus the vehicle's current speed rank, the total of which is then doubled. Before multiplying, increase the total by +1 per 5 feet the landing point is lower than the jump's take off point. A result of 0 or less means the vehicle is not capable of (significantly) jumping at that speed. The jump will also travel a vertical height of one-third (rounded down) as many feet as the jump's distance, with a minimum obtained height of 5 feet. A gargantuan vehicle (defense modifier -4) is trying to make a long leap of 35 feet to leap a chasm using an inclined car trailer as a ramp. The vehicle is moving at speed rank 6 and the driver's maneuver check result is 16, obtaining a vertical jump of 36 feet ((16 - 4) + 6, and then doubled). The vehicle barely jumps over the chasm, reaching a height of 12 feet while doing so. Failing the maneuver skill check means falling short, twisting sideways or the like, or possibly hitting something you are trying to jump over. The vehicle fails to actually become airborne, but must still make a control check to prevent crashing back into the ground, applying a -2 penalty per degree of failure with the maneuver check (keeping in mind this check may not even be possible if the unintended landing spot is on an obstacle or the like). Successfully landing a jump is still likely to damage a vehicle. Depending upon the result of the control check to land the vehicle following a jump, the vehicle may suffer from a slam attack of a damage rank indicated on the Vehicle Jumping Damage table. Anyone inside suffers as though slammed by a Damage modifier half that which is applied to the vehicle.

either.name: Loop
either.summary: The vehicle maneuvers in a vertical circle, returning to its original facing afterward.
either.speed: Reduce speed by half (round down), but falling short of no longer moving.
either.success: the vehicle moves in a circle, moving up or down and then around along the same path of movement to settle back into the same direction.
